segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we ran a straight course and came to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finding a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We came in sight of Cyprus and, leaving it on our left, sailed on to Syria and put in at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When our days there were up, we left and went on our way, and all of them, with wives and children, escorted us until we were outside the city. There we knelt on the beach and prayed

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said farewell to one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they returned to their homes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais, and after greeting the brothers and sisters we stayed with them for one day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day we left and came to Caesarea, and we went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven, and stayed with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While we were staying there for a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘In this way the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is and hand him over into the hands of Gentiles.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we heard this, both we and the local people begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Since he would not be persuaded, we said no more except,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Let the Lord’s will be done.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these days we got ready and began the journey up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the disciples from Caesarea also came with us, bringing us to Mnason, a Cypriot and an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters welcomed us gladly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day Paul went in with us to see James, and all the elders were present.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After greeting them, he recounted one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his service.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they glorified God, and they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands there are among the Jews who have believed, and they are all zealous for the Law.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to the customs.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: What, then, is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So do what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow they took of their own accord.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Take these men, be purified along with them, and pay their expenses so that they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also stay in line and keep the Law.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent word of our decision that they should keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Paul took the men, and on the next day, after being purified along with them, he went into the temple to give notice of when the days of purification would be completed and the offering presented for each one of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the seven days were almost over, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people and the Law and this place. What is more, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian in the city with him, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The whole city was aroused, and the people came running together. They took hold of Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While they were trying to kill him, a report went up to the commander of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At once he took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the commander came up, took hold of him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains; and he began asking who he was and what he had done.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. Since he could not learn anything certain because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken into the barracks.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Paul reached the steps, he had to be carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the mass of the people followed, shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Away with him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the commander,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May I say something to you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He replied,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you know Greek?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Then you are not the Egyptian who some time ago raised a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had given permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. When a great silence had fallen, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

notes.note: These are the seven men chosen in Acts 6 to oversee the daily distribution of food in Jerusalem. This Philip later proclaimed the message in Samaria and to the Ethiopian official (Acts 8), and he is distinct from Philip the apostle, one of the Twelve.
The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” In the plural it regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples and is then rendered “Gentiles.” It is the same word in verses 19, 21 and 25.

The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody. Older versions have “deliver,” and many recent ones have “hand over” here. Luke uses the same verb for Jesus being handed over to the Gentiles (Luke 18:32), and the echo is probably intended.

The Greek is compressed and can also be read as “bringing with them Mnason, with whom we were to lodge,” as some older versions have it. Most modern translations take it as here. “Early disciple” probably means he had belonged to the movement from its first days.

This is James the brother of Jesus, by this time the leading figure in the Jerusalem community (Acts 12:17; 15:13; Galatians 1:19). He is not James the son of Zebedee, whose death is reported in Acts 12:2.

Most translations have “ministry.” In the first century this was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Ministry” now suggests clergy or a church profession.

The head-shaving and the offerings point to a Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which ended with shaving the head and costly sacrifices. Paying for the sacrifices of others who had taken such a vow was a recognized act of piety. Exactly how Paul’s own purification and the seven days of verse 27 fit the procedure is debated.

“Asia” here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, not the continent. Its chief city was Ephesus, where Paul had worked for several years, which is why these Jews recognized both Paul and Trophimus the Ephesian.

Non-Jews could enter the outer court of the temple, but a barrier marked the point beyond which they were forbidden to go on pain of death. Greek inscriptions warning of this have been found. The charge, which verse 29 calls a mistaken assumption, was therefore a capital one.

The Greek title, literally “leader of a thousand,” was the standard equivalent of the Roman military tribune. Here it is the officer in charge of the cohort stationed in Jerusalem, a unit of several hundred to a thousand soldiers. The garrison was housed in the Antonia fortress, which overlooked the temple courts and was joined to them by steps, so the report “went up” and the troops “ran down.”

The Greek borrows the Latin word sicarii, “dagger-men.” It names militants who killed their opponents in crowds with concealed daggers. Josephus also describes an Egyptian prophet who led a large following in the time of the governor Felix and escaped when the Romans attacked. The commander’s words are best read as a surprised inference from Paul’s Greek, though some take them as a question expecting the answer yes.

The phrase may mean Hebrew itself or Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in Judea, which Greek writers could also call “Hebrew.” Many scholars and several translations take it as Aramaic; others argue that Hebrew is meant. The translation keeps the Greek’s own term.

candidates.reason: The plural used of the believing community recurs in nearly every book, and translations split between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers,” so one policy is needed.
It recurs through Acts 21–25 and in the Gospels and Revelation, and translations vary between “tribune,” “commander” and “chief captain.”
It recurs across the Gospels, Acts, Paul and Revelation, with competing renderings (“fornication,” “sexual immorality,” “unchastity”) that readers should see as one word.
The figurative sense of conducting one’s life is frequent in Paul and John, and translators divide between keeping the idiom “walk” and rendering it “live.”
It occurs only here and names a specific group, so the maintainers may prefer the loanword “Sicarii,” since “Assassins” and “terrorists” each carry misleading associations.
